questions.q: What is biodiversity?
questions.a: The variety of life in a region - different plants, animals and microorganisms, their genes and ecosystems.

questions.q: Why are hotspots of biodiversity important?
questions.a: They hold very high species richness, so protecting them saves many species at once.

questions.q: What are endemic species?
questions.a: Species found only in one particular area, like the lion-tailed macaque of the Western Ghats - losing that habitat kills the species.

questions.q: On what basis are organisms classified?
questions.a: On similarities and differences in body design, cell structure, nutrition and evolutionary relationships.

questions.q: Why is classification needed in biology?
questions.a: Millions of species exist; grouping them makes studying, naming and identifying organisms possible.

questions.q: What is the difference between autotrophic and heterotrophic modes used in classification?
questions.a: Autotrophs make their own food (plants); heterotrophs depend on others (animals, fungi) - a basic basis for grouping.

questions.q: Name the five kingdoms of Whittaker's classification.
questions.a: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

questions.q: On what main criteria is the five-kingdom system based?
questions.a: Cell structure (prokaryote/eukaryote), body organisation, cell wall presence and mode of nutrition.

questions.q: Why were bacteria placed in a separate kingdom Monera?
questions.a: They are prokaryotes - no true nucleus or organelles - unlike all other organisms.

questions.q: What are the chief features of kingdom Monera?
questions.a: Prokaryotic, mostly unicellular, cell wall may or may not be present, nutrition autotrophic or heterotrophic.

questions.q: Give two examples of Monera.
questions.a: Bacteria and blue-green algae (cyanobacteria).

questions.q: Name one useful and one harmful Moneran.
questions.a: Useful: Lactobacillus making curd; harmful: cholera-causing bacteria.

questions.q: What characterises kingdom Protista?
questions.a: Unicellular eukaryotes with a true nucleus; nutrition autotrophic or heterotrophic.

questions.q: Give two examples of Protista.
questions.a: Amoeba and Paramecium (also Euglena, Chlamydomonas).

questions.q: How do protists differ from Monerans?
questions.a: Protists have a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles; Monerans are prokaryotes without them.

questions.q: What are the main features of kingdom Fungi?
questions.a: Eukaryotic, mostly multicellular, cell wall of chitin, saprotrophic heterotrophic nutrition.

questions.q: Give two examples of fungi.
questions.a: Mushroom and yeast (also bread mould Rhizopus, Penicillium).

questions.q: Why are fungi called decomposers?
questions.a: They feed on dead organic matter, breaking it down and recycling nutrients.

questions.q: What basis is used to classify Plantae groups?
questions.a: Whether plants have distinct body parts, vascular tissues, seeds, and whether seeds are naked or in fruits.

questions.q: Name the major groups of the plant kingdom in order of evolution.
questions.a: Thallophyta (algae) -> Bryophyta -> Pteridophyta -> Gymnosperms -> Angiosperms.

questions.q: How do angiosperms differ from gymnosperms?
questions.a: Angiosperm seeds are enclosed in fruits; gymnosperm seeds are naked (as in pine).

questions.q: What criterion separates Porifera from Cnidaria?
questions.a: Porifera have pores and no tissues or symmetry; Cnidaria have a body cavity and tentacles with stinging cells.

questions.q: How are vertebrates different from invertebrates?
questions.a: Vertebrates have a backbone (notochord becomes vertebral column) and a dorsal nerve cord; invertebrates lack it.

questions.q: Name two warm-blooded vertebrate groups.
questions.a: Aves (birds) and Mammalia (mammals).

questions.q: What is taxonomic hierarchy?
questions.a: The ranked grouping of organisms from broadest to narrowest: kingdom -> phylum/division -> class -> order -> family -> genus -> species.

questions.q: Which is the smallest unit of classification?
questions.a: Species - a group of organisms that can interbreed naturally.

questions.q: Why is binomial naming used with hierarchy?
questions.a: The two-part scientific name (genus + species) uniquely identifies each species worldwide.

questions.q: What is binomial nomenclature?
questions.a: The two-word scientific naming system: first the genus name, then the species name, both in Latin style.

questions.q: Who introduced binomial nomenclature?
questions.a: Carolus Linnaeus.

questions.q: Write the binomial name of the mango correctly formatted.
questions.a: Mangifera indica - genus capitalised, species in lower case, both in italics.
